title: The Coaching Habit
author: Michael Bungay Stanier
tagline: Say less, ask more & change the way you lead forever — seven questions that coach any team.
oneLiner: Stop giving answers. Ask seven questions — and watch people solve their own problems.
bigIdea: Michael Bungay Stanier's insight: leaders fall into the 'advice monster' — giving answers, fixing problems, creating dependence. The cure is seven questions that turn any conversation into coaching: the Kickstart ('What's on your mind?'), the AWE question ('And what else?'), the Focus ('What's the real challenge here for you?'), the Foundation ('What do you want?'), the Lazy ('How can I help?'), the Strategic ('If you're saying no, what are you saying yes to?'), and the Learning ('What was most useful for you?'). Ask more, tell less, and people grow.
quotes: The advice monster is the leader's default — and it kills learning.
'And what else?' is the best coaching question in the world.
Asking questions creates a moment of choice — it's the difference between training and coaching.

lessons.title: Tame the Advice Monster
lessons.summary: Leaders are trained to give answers — tell, fix, rescue. But every answer you give trains your team to depend on you. The advice monster is driven by three voices: tell-it, save-it, control-it. Taming it means staying curious and asking instead of advising.
lessons.example: When a team member brings a problem, the leader's instinct is 'here's what to do'. The coaching response — 'what do you think?' — builds capability instead of dependency. Stanier's own confession: as a new manager he answered every question his team brought him — until he realised he was training them to bring problems instead of solutions. The first 'what do you think?' he asked instead produced a better answer than his own would have been.
lessons.action: Catch yourself giving an answer before understanding the question. Convert it: 'What do you think?'

lessons.title: The Kickstart: 'What's on your mind?'
lessons.summary: Every coaching conversation starts with 'What's on your mind?' — it surfaces what actually matters to the other person, not what the agenda says. The question respects that the real issue may differ from the scheduled topic. Start with the person, not the plan.
lessons.example: A weekly 1:1 that opens with 'What's on your mind?' quickly surfaces the real project crisis, instead of spending 30 minutes on the agenda nobody cared about. The opening question 'What's on your mind?' works because it hands the agenda to the other person. One team lead reports that starting every one-on-one this way cut meeting time in half — because the real issue surfaced in the first minute instead of the last.
lessons.action: Open your next 1:1 or team conversation with 'What's on your mind?' and genuinely listen.

lessons.title: The AWE Question: 'And what else?'
lessons.summary: 'And what else?' is the highest-leverage question in coaching: it forces the person past their first answer — which is rarely the real one. Asking it repeatedly (two or three times) uncovers deeper issues, better ideas and hidden concerns. It also stops you from jumping in with solutions.
lessons.example: An employee says 'I need more time'. 'And what else?' reveals: 'I don't trust the process.' The second answer is the real problem — and the first was just the surface. The 'and what else?' question, repeated, consistently surfaces a second, deeper answer. In one coaching session, the first answer was 'workload'; the third answer was 'I don't feel trusted' — the real issue, reached only by refusing to settle for the first response.
lessons.action: After someone's first answer, ask 'And what else?' at least twice before you respond with anything.

lessons.title: The Focus Question: 'What's the real challenge here?'
lessons.summary: People often present the surface problem when the real challenge is different — and it's usually a personal one ('for you'). The focus question cuts through: 'What's the real challenge here for you?' It gets to the part the person owns, where change is actually possible.
lessons.example: A team says 'our tools are outdated'. The real challenge for the manager might be 'I don't know how to argue for budget'. The focus question shifts the conversation to what she can act on.
lessons.action: When someone presents a problem, ask: 'What's the real challenge here for you?' and wait for the second, deeper answer.

lessons.title: The Lazy Question: 'How can I help?'
lessons.summary: 'How can I help?' — the lazy question — is actually the efficient one: it stops you from guessing what the person needs and doing the wrong thing. You're not lazy for asking; you're lazy for guessing. The question also surfaces when the other person doesn't need your help at all.
lessons.example: The employee who wants a sounding board, not a solution: 'How can I help?' reveals 'just listen' — saving you from delivering an unwanted lecture. 'How can I help?' forces the other person to name the actual need instead of dumping the whole problem. A manager who switched to this question found his team stopped bringing him every obstacle and started bringing him only the ones that genuinely needed his authority.
lessons.action: Before jumping in to help, ask: 'How can I help?' — and honor the actual answer, even if it's 'just listen'.

lessons.title: The Strategic Question: 'What are you saying yes to?'
lessons.summary: Every 'no' is a 'yes' to something else — and every 'yes' is a 'no' to something else. The strategic question makes the trade-off visible: 'If you're saying no to this, what are you saying yes to?' It forces prioritization and reveals what the person actually values.
lessons.example: The client who keeps saying no to new work: 'what are you saying yes to?' reveals the answer — 'my family time' — and the leader stops pushing and starts respecting. The 'what are you saying yes to?' question makes trade-offs explicit. One client realised she was saying yes to every meeting and no to her core project — the question, not the calendar, revealed the misalignment.
lessons.action: Before accepting or rejecting anything, name the trade-off: what are you saying yes to by saying no to this?

lessons.title: The Learning Question: 'What was most useful?'
lessons.summary: End conversations with 'What was most useful for you?' — it locks in the learning, gives you feedback on your coaching, and turns the conversation into growth. The question is small but transforms meetings from events into lessons.
lessons.example: After a coaching session, the question helps the person articulate what they'll actually take away — and tells you what worked in your approach. Ending every conversation with 'what was most useful?' takes ten seconds and compounds: the other person leaves with the takeaway crystallised, and the coach learns what actually landed. Stanier calls it the cheapest feedback system ever designed.
lessons.action: End your next three conversations with 'What was most useful for you?' — and notice what it changes.

actionPlan: Catch the advice monster — ask instead of tell.
Open with 'What's on your mind?' in your next 1:1.
Ask 'And what else?' twice before responding.
Find the real challenge with the focus question.
Ask 'How can I help?', name your yes/no trade-offs, and close with 'What was most useful?'
caveat: Stanier's 'ask, don't tell — make coaching a daily habit' is the best management micro-book ever — and RadioShack is the warning that asking questions only works when you're ready to hear the answers: the company's leaders had decades of coaching conversations — they asked, they listened, they empathized — and still ran the business into bankruptcy, because the questions never once challenged the core assumption that the stores would keep selling electronics. The caveat: a coaching habit that never asks 'is the whole model still right?' is just a very polite way of not changing. Ask the hard questions — especially the ones that threaten your own position.
